title: Dhammas: the five heaps

segments.voice: Yesterday: dhammas, the hindrances. Five visitors, and your line was it came, it went. Which one showed up most? Day two hundred sixty-one.

Point to yourself. Go ahead. Where did your finger land? Probably the middle of your chest. But is that you? Your chest is a body part. Your feelings are somewhere else. Your thoughts seem to be up in your head. Your memories aren't anywhere you can point to at all. We say I a thousand times a day, and it feels like one solid thing. The Buddha suggested that if you look closely, what you call I comes apart into five heaps. Today's word: khandha.

Khandha means a heap, a bundle, a mass, like a pile of grain or a bundle of sticks. The Buddha taught that what we call a person can be seen as five of them. Form, rupa: the body and the physical world. Feeling, vedana: pleasant, painful, neither, the second foundation. Perception, sanna: recognizing, labeling, that's a cup, that's my friend. Formations, sankhara: intentions, habits, the urges and choices that shape what we do. And consciousness, vinnana: the plain knowing of anything at all. In the Satipatthana Sutta, the instruction for each heap is familiar by now. Such is form, such is its arising, such is its passing away. The same for feeling, perception, formations and consciousness. Why sort yourself into heaps? Because each heap, looked at closely, is changing all the time, and none of them, on its own, is a solid owner in charge of the rest. That's what the Buddha pointed to with the teaching of anatta, not-self. It doesn't say you don't exist. It says the self you assumed, one thing, fixed and in control, isn't found in any of the five. Elsewhere the Buddha gives a set of pictures for them. Form is like a lump of foam on a river. Feeling like a bubble on the water. Perception like a mirage. Formations like the trunk of a banana tree, layer after layer and no hard core. And consciousness like a magician's trick.
screen: `KHANDHA: A HEAP, A BUNDLE.` · `WHAT WE CALL A PERSON: FIVE OF THEM.` · `EACH ONE ARISING AND PASSING.` · `FOAM, BUBBLE, MIRAGE, BANANA TREE, TRICK.` · then, large: `FIVE HEAPS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and pick one moment: a sound, like a car passing. Now sort it into five. Form: the sound waves, your ear. Feeling: pleasant, painful, or neither? Perception: the label, a car. Formations: any urge, wishing it would stop, wondering where it's going. Consciousness: the plain knowing of it all. Five heaps, one moment. Then let it go, and wait for the next one. The bell holds the time.
Khandha. A heap: the Buddha's five, form, feeling, perception, formations and consciousness, each one arising and passing.
Your line: five heaps. Today, when something upsets you, try sorting that one moment into five, and notice whether it feels a little less solid. Day two hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: The five aggregates are taught across all Buddhist schools; practitioners contemplate them to see that each is changing and that no lasting, controlling self is found among them.

match.prompt: match each heap to its picture.
pairs: a lump of foam on a river
a banana tree with no hard core

myth: the teaching of not-self says you don't exist
it says the solid, controlling self you assumed isn't found in any of the five heaps.
khandha literally means a heap or bundle
like a pile of grain or a bundle of sticks.
the Buddha compares consciousness to a magician's trick
one of five pictures for the five heaps.

fork.setup: you hear a car pass. which heap is the label 'that's a car'?
fork.reveal: perception, sanna, is recognizing and labeling. the sound is form, its tone is feeling.

original.note: Pali khandha (Sanskrit skandha): a heap, bundle or aggregate.

trapdoor: what you thought: the five heaps are five parts of a person, like organs.
what it means: five ways experience comes together, each changing, none a solid owner.
what a scholar hears: the foam, bubble, mirage, banana trunk and magic-trick similes come from SN 22.95, the Pheṇapiṇḍūpama Sutta; the Sanskrit form skandha returns in the Heart Sutra.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikāya 10 (Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta), the five aggregates

notes: Not-self framed as 'the solid, controlling self isn't found in the five'; confirm this framing is acceptable (schools differ in emphasis).
SN 22.95 similes: form/foam, feeling/bubble, perception/mirage, formations/plantain trunk, consciousness/magic trick; confirm.
The aggregates return in the Heart Sutra (day 268); the trapdoor points ahead to that.
